content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published a set of consolidated guidelines on differentiated HIV testing services, including a web annex that focuses on facility-based HIV self-testing (FB-HIVST). These guidelines, published under a Creative Commons license, allow for non-commercial use, adaptation, and redistribution, provided proper citation is given. However, the WHO logo cannot be used, and any adaptations must be licensed under similar terms. Translations of the work must include a disclaimer stating that the WHO is not responsible for the accuracy or content of the translation. Since 2016, HIV self-testing (HIVST) has been implemented globally in various settings. In high-burden areas, the use of HIVST in healthcare facilities has shown potential to increase testing uptake and improve efficiency. Facility-based HIVST (FB-HIVST) can also replace risk-based screening tools to prioritize testing. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the benefits and harms of FB-HIVST, comparing it to other HIV testing services offered at facilities, at home, or with no intervention. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and observational studies. Four RCTs involving 4,811 participants compared FB-HIVST to provider-administered rapid HIV testing in facilities. The evidence suggested that FB-HIVST was acceptable and feasible, with no reported social harm. Two observational cohort studies reported that 97.3% of participants found HIVST easy to use, while 2.9% did not. Additional studies indicated that FB-HIVST was cost-effective in high-burden outpatient settings, although costs varied significantly. Common reasons for preferring FB-HIVST included the use of oral fluid-based testing, interest in trying a new method, convenience, and access to in-person support if needed. Support tools, such as in-person demonstrations and instructional resources, were valued by some users. The findings informed the development of WHO guidelines, which recommend FB-HIVST as an additional HIV testing approach, particularly as a replacement for risk-based screening tools. The systematic review assessed the certainty of evidence using the GRADE approach. While FB-HIVST was generally favored, the evidence was downgraded in some cases due to risks of performance bias (lack of blinding), detection bias (self-reported outcomes), and selection bias. Subgroup analyses suggested that heterogeneity in results could be explained by differences in populations (general vs. key populations) and whether participants received sensitization training before the intervention. Overall, FB-HIVST was found to be a safe and effective method to improve HIV testing coverage. It is particularly desirable in high-burden settings and among populations with limited access to traditional testing services. The WHO guidelines emphasize the importance of offering FB-HIVST as an additional option to enhance HIV testing strategies globally.
